<h3>Calendrier</h3><p>Chaque tour fait a:
Calendar

Each turn moves the calendar forward by 4 days without changing the pace of the game: marches, sieges, production, truces and delays therefore take 4 times longer in calendar time (an invasion that used to take 6 months now takes about 2 years). Durations given in days in this help are counted in turns; on screen, they are converted into calendar days (×4). The following remain calendar-based: seasons, annual population growth, the 10 to 15 years per technology level, the 6 months of overextension, the year of vassalage, 2050 and 2100.

Technology level (1 to 4)

It replaces the old equipment generations and multiplies the attack and HP of all units: ×1 at level 1, ×1.35 at level 2, ×1.70 at level 3, ×2.05 at level 4. Start: United States, Israel, South Korea, Japan 3; Taiwan 2.8; France, United Kingdom 2.5; Germany, Canada, Australia 2.4; Sweden 2.3; China, Russia, North Korea and other European countries 2; Turkey, India 1.6; Iran 1.5; Pakistan 1.4; others 1. Each level takes 10 to 15 years (drawn at random) with a budget of 2.5% of GDP devoted to defence and research (about −12.5% of revenue); laboratories and universities speed it up to ×2, and catching up with a level already reached elsewhere is 30% faster. Level 4 is only available after 2050.

Military experience (1 to 3.5)

×1 at level 1, ×1.25 at level 2, ×1.50 at level 3. Start: United States, Israel, Russia 3; Ukraine 2.6; France, United Kingdom 1.6; Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, India 1.4; others 1. Conquests: +0.1 per 10 million inhabitants and +0.1 per 500,000 km² taken by force (half by treaty, nothing by integrating a vassal), divided by the current level and capped at +0.5 per war. Losses: −0.08 per 10 million inhabitants and −0.06 per 500,000 km² (half in case of secession). A victory against a stronger enemy is worth up to +0.02. After 10 years of peace, −0.02 per year. Seasoned formations also gain up to +20%.

Military strength and power index

Military strength = sum, for each unit, of its attack × technology multiplier × experience multiplier, plus conventional missiles. It is used in combat and for tactical decisions. At the start it is calibrated: United States 30% of the world total, China 18%, Russia 10%, India 10%, European Union 8%, rest of the world 24%.

Power index (0 to 100) = weighted geometric mean: military strength 40%, GDP × currency factor 25%, technology level 10%, population 10%, area 5%, intelligence 5%, stability 5%. Alliances: add 80% of the power of your faction's members, 50% of allies', 30% of pacts'. It governs the nuclear doctrine (ultimatums) and appears in the ranking.

The factor multiplies the debt ceiling and divides interest. Starting bonus: one year of revenue for the United States, a year and a half for the petro-monarchies (Saudi Arabia, Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain), six months for the countries of the European Union.

Intelligence

Satellites at the start: United States 160, Russia 75, China 60, then the Europeans (France 14, United Kingdom 10, Germany 9…), the others far behind. Intelligence gives up to +20% attack against observed nations and +18% missile interception. A launch requires a space centre, universities (total level 2), technology level 1.5, 80 💰 and 3 🔩, and takes about 240 turns (more than two and a half calendar years), shortened by universities and the centre's level.

Heavy units

The most powerful units cost more and take longer to produce (growing with their attack: aircraft carrier ×2.2 in cost and ×1.8 in time); carrier strike groups, invasion bombers and spaceships cost twice as much and take 365, 240 and 730 turns (4 years, 2½ years and 8 years in calendar time). Each copy already owned or in production makes the next one 10% more expensive.

Strategic locks (“Great powers” scenario)

The three most populous cities of Russia, the United States, Japan, Indonesia, China and India are locks. As long as an enemy fights in or occupies one, its units there suffer 2.5 times more attrition (1% per turn), 2.5 times higher upkeep and consumption of fuel, ammunition and food, and a loss of morale, while the defender raises resistance infantry proportional to the population every 5 turns (20 days), until liberation. Exception: a crushing invader (forces on site at least 4 times stronger than the defenders and the city's potential resistance, which grows with its population) makes the lock give way. The cities concerned carry 🔒 in their tooltip.

Garrisons

No city is left without troops: when the last formation leaves a city, it leaves a unit behind as a garrison, and any empty city receives an infantry garrison every 10 turns, paid for if the treasury allows.
